## 2.1 Data sources and construction

This study uses farm-level data from the three most recent Ghana Living Standards Surveys: GLSS5, conducted in 2005/06; GLSS6, conducted in 2012/13; and GLSS7, conducted in 2016/17. The GLSS surveys are repeated cross-sectional household surveys that use a two-stage sampling design, with enumeration areas selected in the first stage and households selected in the second stage. We rely on the consolidated farmer-level GLSS dataset developed by @Tsiboe2020, which harmonizes farm production outcomes across survey rounds and has been used to study agricultural productivity across multiple Ghanaian crop value chains [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2021; @Tsiboe2021b; @Tsiboe2021c; @Tsiboe2022]. All monetary values are expressed in constant 2016/17 Ghana cedis using the national consumer price index.

Two conventions on weighting apply, and they differ by purpose. The descriptive statistics in Tables 1 to 5 and S3 to S4 are unweighted. Every comparison they report is made within a survey round, between groups drawn from those same rounds, so the design weight enters both sides of each contrast. Reporting the sample rather than the population also keeps the descriptive tables on the same footing as the estimation sample the frontier is fitted to. The frontier estimation is weighted. The household design weight enters the likelihood, so the technology a farmer is measured against is the technology of the population that farmer represents. Where a statistic in this paper describes the sample it is unweighted; where it describes the frontier it is weighted. The descriptive means are not national estimates and should not be read as such.

Although the consolidated dataset provides harmonized farm-level outcomes, it does not directly contain the community-level agricultural service provision indicators required for this study. To construct these measures, we returned to the agriculture section of the GLSS community questionnaire, which records the service environment of the enumeration area rather than of any individual household, and merged it into the farmer-level data using survey and enumeration-area identifiers. The community questionnaire is administered not to households but to a panel of community opinion leaders, and the survey protocol requires that panel to reflect the occupational, ethnic, gender, and religious composition of the community. Our treatment measures are key-informant reports of what is *available* in a locality. They are not administrative records, and they are not household reports of services *received*. That distinction governs how the estimates should be read, and we return to it below.

Variables are harmonized using GLSS7 as the reference structure, since it is the most recent round and organizes the service questions most clearly. GLSS6 is numbered identically across the relevant block; GLSS5 requires renaming, because it lacks the compliance item and its association, cooperative, and tractor questions therefore sit one position earlier. Where a community contributes more than one record, indicators are collapsed to one observation per survey and enumeration area by taking the maximum, so a service counts as available if any informant record reports it. Appendix Table S1 gives the source question and construction rule for every variable and Table S2 documents the cross-round mapping; Note S1 sets out the harmonization, the collapse rule and their consequences in full. One item is not available in GLSS5 at all: compliance with extension guidance. Every statistic involving it is restricted to GLSS6 and GLSS7, so Table 5 rests on a smaller denominator than Tables 2 to 4, and its note records this.

For the meta-stochastic frontier analysis we define four indicators of the institutional source of service delivery. A community is classified as having: (i) *any service source* if it has an agricultural or fishing association, an agricultural cooperative, or active extension; (ii) an *association* source if an agricultural or fishing association is present; (iii) a *cooperative* source if farmers participate in an agricultural cooperative; and (iv) an *active extension* source if an extension officer visits farmers in the community. These are four separate binary treatments, each estimated against its own pair of group-specific frontiers, rather than four levels of a single categorical treatment. A second set of indicators captures the *content* of services available: planting or seed-use support, mechanization, credit, irrigation, animal husbandry, fertilizer and other agrochemical inputs, post-harvest, marketing or storage support, communal labour, employment, and record-keeping. These enter the analysis as a disaggregation of the estimated gap rather than as treatments.

Three construction decisions behind these indicators bear on how the results should be read. Each is derived in Note S1, against the questionnaire items listed in Table S1 and mapped across rounds in Table S2. First, the content indicators are not all drawn from the same question: the questionnaire carries separate rosters for the services an extension agent provides and for those an association provides, so three indicators come from one roster, three from the other, and the remainder from either. A reader comparing irrigation against credit in Table 4 is comparing an extension-only measure with a pooled one. Second, active extension requires a threshold, because the underlying variable runs from no extension presence at all through office, stationed officer, and visits together. We classify a community as having active extension when an officer visits, which is the partition above which farmer-facing contact occurs, and the choice is not close-run because the passive states are nearly empty against the `r tbl_pct("table3", "share/Pooled", "v3", 0)` of farmers in communities where an officer visits and no other infrastructure is present. Section 5 reports the estimates under a stricter definition that also excludes the passive states from the comparison group.

Third, the comparison group for the three source-specific treatments departs from the siblings. A community that has no association but does have a cooperative or active extension is set to missing rather than zero, and drops out of the association comparison entirely; the same applies to the cooperative and active-extension contrasts. Such a community is *treated under a different arm*, not untreated, and coding it zero would place served farms in the reference group and contaminate the frontier the treated group is measured against. Each estimate is therefore a difference against communities with no agricultural service source of any kind rather than against other service arrangements. The rule is not costless: of the `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$prevalence$n_all), 0)` farm observations, the association contrast retains `r fmt_num(sum(unlist(objs$prevalence$n_obs$services1)), 0)`, the cooperative contrast `r fmt_num(sum(unlist(objs$prevalence$n_obs$services2)), 0)`, and the active-extension contrast `r fmt_num(sum(unlist(objs$prevalence$n_obs$services3)), 0)`. Because all four contrasts retain the same comparison group, their estimates are not statistically independent and should not be pooled or differenced as if drawn from separate samples. Section 5 reports a robustness arm in which excluded communities are coded zero instead.

Under these definitions, `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$services0$GLSS5), 1)` of farmers in GLSS5 lived in a community with at least one agricultural service source, `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$services0$GLSS6), 1)` in GLSS6 and `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$services0$GLSS7), 1)` in GLSS7. That is a stable majority rather than a trend. The composition beneath it is not stable. Active extension reaches `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$extension_officer_visit$GLSS5), 1)`, `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$extension_officer_visit$GLSS6), 1)` and `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$extension_officer_visit$GLSS7), 1)` of farmers across the three rounds; association presence falls from `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$farm_association$GLSS5), 1)` to `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$farm_association$GLSS7), 1)`; and cooperative participation moves non-monotonically, from `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$community_cooperative$GLSS5), 1)` to `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$community_cooperative$GLSS6), 1)` and back to `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$community_cooperative$GLSS7), 1)`. A constant headline share is consistent with substantial churn in how service is delivered. That is the paper's reason for treating the four sources separately rather than as one aggregate.

Unless otherwise stated, terms such as *"association community"* or *"community with active extension"* in this paper refer to this community-level classification. Every sampled farmer residing in a classified enumeration area is treated as exposed, regardless of whether that farmer personally received a service, belonged to the association, or met an extension officer. This is the paper's central interpretive commitment: the estimates describe the effect of operating in a service-provisioned locality, not of individual programme participation, and they will understate the difference between participants and non-participants to the extent that provision and uptake diverge.

Three features of the instrument bound what these measures can support. Service provision is reported by community informants, so the treatment records availability rather than receipt, and a community counted as served may contain farmers who never used the service. The service-content items are asked only where a provider exists, so their absence for unserved communities is assigned by construction rather than measured, and content contrasts compare a measured category against a definitional one. That is the only design the questionnaire's skip pattern permits. And implausible values are set to missing before the community-level collapse: extension distances of 999 kilometres or more, and tractor counts of 99 or more, are treated as non-responses rather than as observations. Both rules are applied to the community record rather than to the farm, so a single suppressed community removes the variable for every farm in its enumeration area.

Neither suppression rule bites hard, removing `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$suppression$distance$suppressed) + assert_present(objs$suppression$tractors$suppressed), 0)` records between them out of the `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$suppression$records), 0)` behind GLSS5 to GLSS7. Ordinary item non-response on the same two questions is a larger matter by an order of magnitude, and Note S1 reports both sets of counts. Distance to the nearest extension office is unobserved for close to a quarter of communities, which is why it enters this study as a descriptive covariate and never as a treatment or a frontier input.

The analysis is restricted to crop farmers with reported yields, measured in kilograms per hectare, between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within each survey round and crop. The final sample includes `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$prevalence$n_all), 0)` farm operators: `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$prevalence$n$GLSS5), 0)` in GLSS5, `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$prevalence$n$GLSS6), 0)` in GLSS6 and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$prevalence$n$GLSS7), 0)` in GLSS7. Each cultivates at least one of the following crops: banana, beans, cashew, cassava, citrus fruits, cocoa, coconut, cocoyam, cotton, kenaf, maize, millet, oil palm, peanuts, plantain, potato, rice, sorghum, yam, sugarcane, tomato, pepper, okra, onion, eggplant, and other reported crops.

## 2.2 Descriptive statistics

Table 1 summarises crop producers in Ghana, pooled and disaggregated by whether any agricultural service source is available in the farmer's community; Tables S3 and S4 repeat the exercise for each of the three service sources separately, in levels and in trends. Of the `r fmt_num(tbl_n("table1", "pooled"), 0)` farm operators in the analysis sample, `r fmt_num(tbl_n("table1", "1"), 0)` are in served communities and `r fmt_num(tbl_n("table1", "0"), 0)` are not. Throughout these tables a dagger marks a service-status term that is significant at the ten percent level in the trend model behind the row, not a test of the raw difference in means; on a sample of this size a difference can be large and carry no dagger, or small and carry one, and we describe magnitudes rather than lean on the marker.

The two groups are close on who farms and further apart on what they produce with. Women are `r tbl_pct("table1", "Female farmer (dummy)", "m0", 0)` of operators in unserved communities and `r tbl_pct("table1", "Female farmer (dummy)", "m1", 0)` in served ones, a difference of no practical consequence. Operators in served communities are about a year older (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Age (years)", "m1"), 1)` years against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Age (years)", "m0"), 1)`) and have roughly nine months more schooling (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Education (years)", "m1"), 2)` years against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Education (years)", "m0"), 2)`), the largest proportional gap among the farmer characteristics. Households are marginally smaller in served communities (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Size (AE)", "m1"), 2)` adult equivalents against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Size (AE)", "m0"), 2)`) and dependency ratios are indistinguishable at about `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Dependency (ratio)", "mp"), 2)`. None of this suggests that service provision follows the demographic composition of a community; it suggests, if anything, that it follows something the demographic composition does not capture.

Production and input use tell a different story. Output per hectare across all crops averages GH₵`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "All crops (real GH₵/ha)", "m1"), 0)` in served communities against GH₵`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "All crops (real GH₵/ha)", "m0"), 0)` in unserved ones, a gap of about nine percent. The same ordering holds for most individual crops, maize (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Maize (Kg/ha)", "m1"), 0)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Maize (Kg/ha)", "m0"), 0)` kg/ha), millet (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Millet (Kg/ha)", "m1"), 0)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Millet (Kg/ha)", "m0"), 0)`), cassava, cocoyam and plantain among them. Yam runs the other way and by a wide margin (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Yam (Kg/ha)", "m0"), 0)` kg/ha unserved against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Yam (Kg/ha)", "m1"), 0)` served), as do pepper and tomato. Farms in served communities are slightly smaller (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Land (ha)", "m1"), 2)` hectares against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Land (ha)", "m0"), 2)`) and use somewhat more planting material per hectare. What is most striking is how little of the input differential is technological. Only `r tbl_pct("table1", "Irrigation (dummy)", "mp", 0)` of farmers report irrigation, `r tbl_pct("table1", "Mechanization (dummy)", "mp", 0)` mechanized services and `r tbl_pct("table1", "Credit (dummy)", "mp", 0)` credit, and the served-unserved differences in all three are one percentage point or less. These are the technologies a technology gap could plausibly reflect, and at these levels of access there is very little of them in either group to differ over.

Disaggregating by source, in Tables S3 and S4, shows that the sources are not interchangeable. Farmers in extension communities (n = `r fmt_num(tbl_n("tableS3", "ext"), 0)`) and association communities (n = `r fmt_num(tbl_n("tableS3", "assoc"), 0)`) both out-produce the pooled average for most crops, but they are distinguished in different ways. The association group stands out on schooling, at `r fmt_num(tbl_val("tableS3", "Education (years)", "assoc"), 2)` years against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("tableS3", "Education (years)", "pooled"), 2)` pooled, the largest educational gap anywhere in the descriptive tables. The extension group stands out on scale and mechanization. The cooperative group (n = `r fmt_num(tbl_n("tableS3", "coop"), 0)`) is the smallest and the most erratic across crops: its cocoyam and okra cells sit far above the pooled means and its rice and beans cells far below, on cell counts that do not support a reading either way. We note the pattern and decline to interpret it, which is the same restraint the sibling literature has had to exercise where crop cells thin out.

The trends in Table S4 matter more than the levels for what follows, because they run in the direction that makes a cross-sectional comparison hardest to read. Output per hectare grew across the period in both groups but faster where services were present (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "All crops (real GH₵/ha)", "t1"), 2)` percent a year against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "All crops (real GH₵/ha)", "t0"), 2)` percent), and schooling did the same (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Education (years)", "t1"), 2)` percent against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Education (years)", "t0"), 2)` percent). Credit access fell for everyone, and fastest in unserved communities (`r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Credit (dummy)", "t0"), 2)` percent a year against `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Credit (dummy)", "t1"), 2)` percent). Irrigation grew at `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table1", "Irrigation (dummy)", "tp"), 2)` percent a year pooled, from a base low enough that the growth changes nothing about access. Read together, the levels and the trends describe groups that are diverging on the endowments most associated with performance, not converging.

Two things follow, and they set up the rest of the paper. First, served and unserved communities differ systematically on characteristics that independently predict farm performance, so the raw differences in this section cannot be read as the contribution of agricultural services; they require a comparison between farmers who are alike on what we observe, which is what the matched design in Section 4 constructs. Second, the differences are not uniform across the four sources. Association communities differ from unserved ones in one way and extension communities in another, so a single average difference would conceal the structure it is meant to describe. That is the case for a meta-frontier, which separates the technology a group can reach from the efficiency with which it is used, and estimates both separately by source. Section 3 first sets out what agricultural service delivery in Ghana actually consists of, and Section 4 then specifies the estimator.
